title: Review: Internal energy and energy transfers; Particle model and pressure; Atoms and isotopes

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Specific latent heat of fusion
items.clue: The energy per kilogram needed for melting.

items.label: Specific latent heat of vaporisation
items.clue: The energy per kilogram needed for boiling.

items.label: Gas pressure
items.clue: Caused by moving molecules colliding with the walls of their container.

questions.stem: Heating a system increases the energy of the particles that make it up. Which pair of outcomes does the specification give for this?

options.text: It always raises the temperature of the system, without exception
It raises the temperature and it always changes state as well
It raises the pressure or else it produces a change of state
It raises the temperature or it produces a change of state

questions.explanation: This is what the specification states: heating either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state.

questions.stem: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what do the symbols c and ∆θ stand for?

options.text: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the final temperature
c is the specific latent heat and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the temperature change
c is the capacity of the container and ∆θ is a state change

questions.explanation: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, c is specific heat capacity in J/kg °C and ∆θ is the temperature change in °C.

questions.stem: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts at constant temperature?

options.text: Their kinetic energy, because the particles must be moving faster
Their thermal energy, as heat flows into the solid and is stored
Neither store, because the temperature is not changing at all
Their potential energy, as the particles are pulled apart

questions.explanation: The energy supplied separates the particles against the forces between them, raising their potential energy store.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?

options.text: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.
It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
It rises briefly, then falls back to its old value.

questions.explanation: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure exerted: the faster molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature. Using the particle model, why does the pressure decrease?

options.text: Each molecule strikes the wall more gently, since it now has less kinetic energy.
The molecules cool down as they spread out into the much larger space.
The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions.
The molecules shrink in size once they are given more room to move about.

questions.stem: A beaker of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater until all the ice has melted. What does the heating do during that time?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the ice steadily as it melts
It increases the energy stored and produces a change of state
The energy stored stays the same as the temperature holds steady
It has no effect until the ice reaches its melting point

questions.explanation: The energy supplied increases the energy of the particles and produces the change of state from solid to liquid.

questions.stem: In which of these situations does the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ apply?

options.text: While ice at 0 °C melts into water that is also at 0 °C
While water at 100 °C is boiling away steadily into steam
While water at 0 °C freezes solid inside a freezer
While the water in a kettle warms from 20 °C up to 90 °C

questions.explanation: The temperature of the water is changing with no change of state, which is when ∆E = m c ∆θ applies.

questions.stem: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific latent heat of a substance?

options.text: The energy needed to change the state of a whole sample of it
The energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
The energy needed to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
The energy needed to change one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius

questions.explanation: This is the definition: the energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.

questions.stem: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?

options.text: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.
The molecules swelling up and pressing against the walls.
The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.

questions.explanation: Gas pressure comes from the huge number of collisions the randomly moving molecules make with the walls each second, each collision exerting a small force.

questions.stem: Under which conditions does the relationship pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?

options.text: Any mass of gas at all, whatever its temperature happens to be doing.
A fixed mass of gas whose temperature is steadily climbing.
Any gas at all, so long as its container has been sealed.
A fixed mass of gas that is being held at a constant temperature.

questions.explanation: The specification introduces the relationship with exactly this condition: for a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant.

questions.stem: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, which units does the specification give for ∆E and for ∆θ?

options.text: ∆E is in joules, J, and ∆θ is in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules per second, and ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in joules per kilogram, J/kg
∆E in joules, and ∆θ in J/kg °C

questions.explanation: The specification gives change in thermal energy, ∆E, in joules, J, and temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius, °C.

questions.stem: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state?

options.text: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat × ∆θ
energy for a state change = mass ÷ specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
energy for a change of state = mass × specific heat capacity

questions.explanation: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as E = m L.
